case.display_title: Tired and off her food after the flu, with failing kidneys

clock.day_0_label: Admission work-up (admitted on 11 March 2025; first laboratory results 12 March)

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to see a 60-year-old woman with severe oliguric acute kidney injury after an influenza-like illness. We reviewed the Chart so far. The degree of uraemia and the low urine output are indications for urgent haemodialysis. The kidney injury is accompanied by anaemia and markers of haemolysis, so a pigment-related or microangiopathic cause needs to be considered alongside glomerular disease. The cause is not yet clear. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Start haemodialysis now through a temporary dialysis catheter
Urinalysis with microscopy, urine protein:creatinine ratio and urine myoglobin
Kidney ultrasound with renal artery and vein Doppler
Blood film for red cell fragments, ADAMTS13 activity and creatine kinase
ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM, complement and serum protein studies
Plan a kidney biopsy once the platelet count and clotting allow, if the cause remains unclear

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise; the Chart now includes the kidney biopsy. It shows haemoglobin cast nephropathy with acute tubular injury, haemosiderin in the tubular epithelium and thrombi in intrarenal veins, with normal glomeruli. This is haem-pigment tubular injury from intravascular haemolysis, not a glomerulonephritis, and the venous thrombi suggest a prothrombotic haemolytic process. Recovery of urine output is encouraging. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Ask again about previous episodes of dark urine
Look for the cause of intravascular haemolysis with thrombosis with haematology, including high-sensitivity PNH flow cytometry
Leg vein ultrasound, given the venous thrombi and the raised D-dimer
Watch the biopsy site: check for a perirenal haematoma before full anticoagulation
Continue dialysis only as needed while the kidney recovers

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on anaemia with haemolysis and severe acute kidney injury. We reviewed the Chart so far. There is haemolysis with an inappropriately low reticulocyte response, which suggests the marrow is also involved. A positive direct antiglobulin test on its own does not establish autoimmune haemolysis, particularly with C3d and no spherocytes. If the film shows no red cell fragments and ADAMTS13 activity is not severely reduced, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is unlikely. The cause is not yet clear. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Urine haemosiderin, plasma free haemoglobin and haptoglobin to look for intravascular haemolysis
Red cell eluate and antibody screen
Ask about previous episodes of dark urine
Consider PNH flow cytometry, ideally with a high-sensitivity FLAER-based method and before further transfusion
B12, folate and iron studies
No rituximab or other escalation of immunosuppression on the DAT alone

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise; the Chart now includes a kidney biopsy with haemoglobin casts, tubular haemosiderin and intrarenal venous thrombi. Chronic intravascular haemolysis with venous thrombosis and a poor marrow response is the key combination here, and the positive DAT is better explained by complement fragments on the red cells than by an autoantibody. A normal conventional CD55/CD59 result would not be reassuring: that method and its gating can miss an abnormal cell population, and transfusion dilutes abnormal red cells. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: High-sensitivity PNH flow cytometry with FLAER on peripheral blood (granulocytes and red cells)
Leg vein ultrasound; anticoagulate once the biopsy site is stable
Bone marrow aspirate, trephine and marrow flow cytometry
Folic acid; transfuse washed red cells only if needed
Stop steroids if the DAT remains the only reason for them

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise; the Chart now includes high-sensitivity PNH flow cytometry with a granulocyte PNH clone of 98.46% and red cells 3.06% (after transfusion). This result, with intravascular haemolysis, haemoglobin cast nephropathy and venous thrombosis, accounts for the whole picture, including the kidney injury and the positive DAT. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Meningococcal vaccination (with antibiotic cover if treatment cannot wait two weeks) before a complement C5 inhibitor
Start a complement C5 inhibitor (eculizumab) once vaccinated
Continue anticoagulation for the iliac vein thrombosis
Stop steroids
Folic acid; iron only if iron deficiency develops
Send PIGA sequencing to support the result, if available

consult_notes.note_text: Asked whether a connective tissue disease or vasculitis could explain acute kidney injury with haemolysis and a positive direct antiglobulin test. We reviewed the Chart so far. There are no joint, skin, mucosal or respiratory features of lupus or vasculitis, and if ANA, anti-dsDNA and ANCA are negative with normal complement, a systemic autoimmune cause is unlikely. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Anti-GBM antibodies if not done
A kidney biopsy will settle whether there is a glomerulonephritis
No immunosuppression from a rheumatology point of view

consult_notes.note_text: Asked whether an infection explains acute kidney injury and haemolysis after influenza A. We reviewed the Chart so far. She is afebrile with a normal procalcitonin and only a slightly raised CRP. There is no travel or animal exposure suggesting leptospirosis or malaria, and the loose stools are not bloody. We see no active infection to explain the picture. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Blood, urine and stool cultures
Malaria antigen test and leptospira serology only if the exposure history changes
No antibiotics on current evidence

accepted_differential: Warm or mixed autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (positive DAT)
Thrombotic microangiopathy: TTP, HUS after diarrhoea, or complement-mediated (atypical) HUS
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis or ANCA vasculitis
Drug-induced or infection-associated haemolysis and AKI (after influenza)
Aplastic anaemia or another marrow failure syndrome
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (platelets falling on dialysis heparin, and to 45 x10^9/L after LMWH was started)

secondary_findings: Positive DAT (IgG and C3d), most likely complement fragment deposition from ongoing complement activation, not autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Right iliac vein thrombosis and intrarenal venous thrombosis
Inappropriately low reticulocyte count and falling platelets: marrow involvement
Small perirenal haematoma after the kidney biopsy
final_dx.text: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria presenting as dialysis-dependent acute kidney injury from haemoglobin cast nephropathy, with a positive DAT (IgG and C3d), intrarenal and right iliac venous thrombosis, and a falsely normal conventional CD55/CD59 flow cytometry from a method or gating problem (transfusion also dilutes the red cell clone)

key_discriminators: urine blood 2+ with few red cells
haemoglobin casts with tubular haemosiderin on biopsy

must_do.text: Dialyse urgently for oliguric AKI with uraemia and hyperkalaemia
Ask specifically about previous episodes of dark urine
Exclude a thrombotic microangiopathy: blood film for fragments and ADAMTS13 activity
Obtain a kidney biopsy to establish the cause of the AKI

Send high-sensitivity FLAER-based flow cytometry on granulocytes, and do not accept a normal conventional CD55/CD59 result, which can be falsely normal from its method or gating (transfusion also dilutes the red cell clone)
Look for venous thrombosis and anticoagulate once the biopsy site allows
Vaccinate against meningococcus before starting a complement C5 inhibitor, then start it

must_not_do.text: Escalate immunosuppression for presumed autoimmune haemolysis on the DAT alone (rituximab, cytotoxics, splenectomy)
Start plasma exchange for presumed TTP with no red cell fragments and ADAMTS13 activity of 53%
Start a complement inhibitor without meningococcal vaccination
Exclude the diagnosis on a normal conventional CD55/CD59 result without a high-sensitivity test

ground_truth.outcome: Haematological remission and progressive renal recovery: haemoglobin, LDH, creatinine and platelets returned to normal over seven months of follow-up (values only in Figure 1).

rubric.text: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, with the kidney injury attributed to haemolysis (haemoglobin cast nephropathy)
Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, without explaining the kidney injury
Haem-pigment nephropathy or tubular necrosis from intravascular haemolysis, cause not identified
Autoimmune haemolysis, a thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP, HUS or complement-mediated HUS), rhabdomyolysis or aplastic anaemia as the final diagnosis
Unrelated diagnosis, or one that would lead to harm

teaching_points: Dark urine with dipstick blood but few red cells on microscopy means haemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria; the CK separates them.
Haemolysis with a low reticulocyte count points to marrow involvement, not isolated autoimmune haemolysis.
A positive DAT (including C3d) can occur in complement-mediated haemolysis; it does not establish AIHA on its own.

Conventional CD55/CD59 flow cytometry can be falsely normal from its method or gating, even with a large clone; transfusion also dilutes the red cell clone, but cannot normalise neutrophils. High-sensitivity FLAER-based testing on granulocytes is the standard.
Kidney biopsy with haemoglobin casts and tubular haemosiderin identifies haem-pigment injury and can redirect the work-up.
Vaccinate against meningococcus (or give antibiotic cover) before complement C5 inhibition.
ground_truth.treatment_given: Emergency haemodialysis (12-16 March), four units of washed red cells, empirical methylprednisolone 40 mg/day from 19 March (stopped 21 April). Prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin 5,000 IU daily from 23 March because of a small post-biopsy perirenal haematoma, then therapeutic rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily from 2 April. Meningococcal vaccination at the patient's request before eculizumab, started 21 April (600 mg weekly for four weeks, then 900 mg every two weeks).

raw_material.findings: No thrombosis in the renal arteries or veins.

Tubular epithelial necrosis and sloughing with necrotic debris in tubular lumina; haemosiderin granules in tubular epithelial cytoplasm (H&E); glomeruli unremarkable (PAM); blue intracytoplasmic granules in tubular epithelium (Prussian blue); electron-dense granules in tubular lumina (electron microscopy). Reported as haemoglobin cast nephropathy with thrombosis in intrarenal veins.

reports.impression: Anaemia without red cell fragments or spherocytes.
reports.report_text: Red cells are normocytic with mild anisocytosis. No red cell fragments (schistocytes 0%). No spherocytes, agglutination or polychromasia. White cells are normal in number and morphology. Platelets are adequate in number.

reports.impression: No fragments or spherocytes; reticulocyte response inappropriately low.
reports.report_text: Film reviewed by a haematopathologist. Red cells are normocytic with mild anisocytosis. No red cell fragments, spherocytes, agglutination or inclusions. Polychromasia is not increased, which is inappropriate for the degree of anaemia. White cells and platelets show no morphological abnormality. Comment: the absence of fragments argues against a microangiopathic process; correlate with haemolysis markers, including urine haemosiderin and plasma free haemoglobin.

reports.impression: Bilaterally enlarged kidneys, as in acute kidney injury; no obstruction.
reports.report_text: Both kidneys are enlarged, with increased cortical echogenicity and preserved corticomedullary differentiation. No hydronephrosis and no calculi. The bladder is collapsed around a catheter.

reports.impression: No renal artery or renal vein thrombosis.
reports.report_text: Both renal arteries and main renal veins are patent with normal flow. No thrombus is seen. Intrarenal resistive indices are raised at 0.78-0.80.

reports.impression: Haemoglobin cast nephropathy with acute tubular injury and tubular haemosiderin deposition; thrombosis in intrarenal veins.
reports.report_text: Percutaneous kidney biopsy. Light microscopy: the glomeruli are unremarkable (PAM). There is tubular epithelial necrosis with sloughing and detachment, and necrotic debris in the tubular lumina. Haemosiderin granules are seen in the cytoplasm of tubular epithelial cells (H&E); Prussian blue staining shows blue intracytoplasmic granules in the tubular epithelium. Pigmented casts in the tubules are consistent with haemoglobin casts. Thrombi are present in intrarenal veins. Immunofluorescence: no glomerular immune deposits; the casts show no light-chain restriction. Electron microscopy: electron-dense granules within the tubular lumina.
Echogenic thrombus in the right iliac vein with absent flow. The right common femoral, femoral and popliteal veins are compressible with phasic flow. The left leg veins are patent and compressible.

reports.impression: Partial loss of CD16 on granulocytes and CD14 on monocytes; no blast excess.
reports.report_text: Bone marrow flow cytometry. Granulocytes show partial reduction of CD16 expression and monocytes show partial loss of CD14 expression; these antigens share a GPI anchor. No increase in CD34-positive blasts; lymphocytes show a normal T, B and NK distribution; plasma cells are not increased. Comment: suggest high-sensitivity flow cytometry with FLAER on peripheral blood.

reports.impression: Mildly hypocellular marrow with an inadequate erythroid response; no dysplasia or excess blasts.
reports.report_text: Particulate aspirate, mildly hypocellular for age. Erythropoiesis is normoblastic and present but not increased despite the anaemia. Granulopoiesis matures normally; megakaryocytes are present in normal numbers with normal morphology. No dysplasia and no increase in blasts (1%). No infiltrate.

reports.impression: Mildly hypocellular marrow; no fibrosis or infiltrate.
reports.report_text: Adequate trephine core, mildly hypocellular for age (about 30%), with trilineage haematopoiesis. No fibrosis on reticulin stain. No infiltrate, granulomas or excess blasts.

reports.impression: Storage iron present; no ring sideroblasts.
reports.report_text: Perls stain shows storage iron present (grade 2) in marrow fragments. No ring sideroblasts.
Twenty metaphases analysed. 46,XX. No clonal abnormality detected.
Two hundred interphase nuclei scored per probe. Normal signal patterns for 5q31, 7q31, chromosome 8 centromere and 20q12.
Targeted sequencing of a myeloid gene panel with adequate coverage. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants detected in the genes on this panel.

reports.impression: Enlarged kidneys; otherwise normal. No splenomegaly; hepatic and portal veins patent.
reports.report_text: The liver is normal in size and echotexture. The gallbladder is normal without calculi; the bile ducts are not dilated. The spleen is normal in size (10.5 cm). The pancreas is unremarkable. Both kidneys are enlarged without hydronephrosis. The hepatic and portal veins are patent. No free fluid.
PA chest radiograph. Heart size normal. The lungs are clear; no pleural effusion and no features of pulmonary oedema.

Transthoracic echocardiogram. Normal left ventricular size and systolic function (LVEF 60%). Normal valves. Normal right ventricle; estimated pulmonary artery pressure not raised. No pericardial effusion. IVC normal in size with respiratory variation.

reports.impression: Enlarged kidneys; no obstruction or other abdominal abnormality on a non-contrast study.
reports.report_text: Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis (contrast withheld because of acute kidney injury). Both kidneys are enlarged with mild perinephric stranding; no hydronephrosis or calculi. Liver, spleen, pancreas and adrenal glands normal. No lymphadenopathy. No free fluid. Vascular patency cannot be assessed without contrast.

reports.impression: Enlarged kidneys; no calculi or obstruction.
reports.report_text: Non-contrast CT of the urinary tract. Both kidneys are enlarged with mild perinephric stranding. No calculi, hydronephrosis or hydroureter. The bladder is decompressed around a catheter.
